title: Mexico's Population Growth Slows to Two-Decade Low: INEGI
text:
Mexico's Population Growth Slows to Two-Decade Low: INEGI

 

# Mexico's Population Growth Slows to Two-Decade Low: INEGI

Photo by: Unsplash 

 By Sergio Arturo Lievano Madrigal Journalist 

 Wed, 09/23/2026 10:30 

Mexico's population reached 130.9 million in 2025, but annual growth slowed to 0.7%, the lowest in two decades, as the total fertility rate fell to 1.2 and the median age rose to 32, according to INEGI. Half of Mexican households now receive non-labor income, with social program coverage reaching 41.4%, which increases fiscal and social security pressures. 

Mexico's population reached 130.9 million as of Oct. 15, 2025. That is 4.8 million more than in 2020, according to the final results of the Intercensal Survey 2025 by the National Institute of Statistics and Geography (INEGI). Average annual growth slowed to 0.7%, the lowest rate since 2005–2010, as fertility continues to decline and the median age rises to 32.

The slowdown describes a population that is still expanding, but by smaller increments each year. "The population of Mexico continues to grow in absolute terms. The average annual growth rate is positive, but the population is growing at an increasingly slower pace," says Mauricio Rodríguez, Head of the Sociodemographic Statistics Unit, INEGI. From the 2020 Population and Housing Census to the 2025 survey, the population living in private dwellings grew at an average annual rate of 0.7%. Between 2015 and 2020 that rate was 1%. Mexico remains the 11th most populous country in the world.

The survey also shows a shift in age structure. In 2020, half of the population was 29 or younger. By 2025, the median age had reached 32. Women accounted for 51.9% of the population and men for 48.1%. "There is a reduction in the youngest age groups. There is an increasingly smaller proportion of children and adolescents and a greater proportion of older people, which is associated with the increase in the median age," says Rodríguez. 

Regional gaps remain wide. Chiapas has the youngest population, with a median age of 26. Mexico City has the oldest, at 37. Fertility indicators point the same way. The average number of live-born children among women aged 12 and older fell from 2.1 in 2020 to 1.9 in 2025. The gap by education level persists: women with no schooling reported an average of 4.9 children, while those with upper secondary or higher education reported 1.2. The total fertility rate fell from 1.9 children per woman in 2019 to 1.2 in 2024. Chiapas recorded the highest rate in 2024 at 1.8, followed by Guerrero at 1.6, and Durango and Zacatecas at 1.5 each. Queretaro reported 1.1, Baja California 1.0, and Mexico City had the lowest rate in the country at 0.8.

These results add to earlier official projections of an aging population. The National Population Council's National Population Program 2026-2030 projects that within eight years, people over 60 will outnumber children under 12, and that seniors will make up just under 25% of the population by 2050, close to double today's 13.2%. 

The survey also records changes in households and income. Between 2020 and 2025, the number of inhabited private dwellings rose from 35.2 million to 39.7 million, an average annual growth rate of 2.2%. Average occupants per dwelling fell from 3.6 to 3.3.

Marital status data follow a similar pattern. The share of people aged 12 and older who reported being single rose from 33.7% to 36.2%. The married share fell from 35.3% to 31.8%, and the share in consensual unions stayed at 18.4%.

Income sources show the largest change. The proportion of households in which at least one member received monetary income from sources other than work rose from 38.5% to 50.1%, an increase of 11.6 percentage points. Households receiving income from social programs rose from 25% to 41.4%. Households receiving retirement or pension income rose from 13% to 16.6%, making pensions the second non-labor income source to increase.

For the health sector, an older population shifts demand toward chronic and long-term care. INEGI values unpaid caregiving at 26.3% of GDP, and nearly 70% of older adults in Mexico live with multiple chronic conditions, such as diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia. The same report cites the National Institute of Geriatrics, which says people aged 65 and older now outnumber children under five. 

For the labor market, smaller young cohorts coincide with existing difficulties absorbing young workers. Close to 14.9 million people aged 15 to 29 face exclusion from education, precarious work, poverty, or educational lag, according to the Youth with Decent Work Alliance. The same edition cites an Inter-American Development Bank estimate that Mexico's real labor gap reached 10.4 million people, or 15.7% of the potential labor force.

INEGI collected the Intercensal Survey 2025 between Oct. 6 and Nov. 14, 2025, from a sample of just over 7.3 million inhabited private dwellings. It provides data on the size, composition, and distribution of the population and housing across all 32 states, 2,478 municipalities or territorial demarcations, and localities with 50,000 or more inhabitants. INEGI conducted the exercise at the midpoint between the 2020 and 2030 Population and Housing Censuses, per its launch announcement. The results form the updated baseline for population estimates until the next census.

Av. Paseo de la Reforma 180, piso 20, Col. Juárez, Cuahutémoc, 06600, Ciudad de México.
